item.title: Trump Flaunts Camaraderie With Xi and Putin but Has Little to Show for It
item.description: President Trump called Russia’s leader his “friend” and marveled at China’s warm welcome for his first-ever trilateral summit. But there were no breakthroughs on nuclear control, the war in Ukraine or A.I.
item.dc:creator: Katie Rogers and David E. Sanger
item.media:description: President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, President Xi Jinping of China and President Trump before their trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.

item.title: A Summit Gives Putin the Win He Craves: Equal Stature With Superpowers
item.description: Standing alongside the U.S. and Chinese leaders, President Vladimir V. Putin secured a symbolic triumph in his long quest to restore Russia’s place as a global power.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sonne
item.media:description: Presidents Vladimir V. Putin, Xi Jinping, and Trump in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, in the first meeting ever held between the three countries’ leaders.

item.title: At Summit With Xi and Putin, Trump Seeks to Project Power Abroad While Sharing It at Home
item.description: Weakened by the midterm elections, President Trump offered hugs, arm pats and smiles to autocrats from Russia and China in contrast to the threats he is making to ascendant Democrats in Washington.
item.dc:creator: Peter Baker
item.media:description: A trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday offered a welcome respite to President Trump, who has long expressed admiration for authoritarian leaders like President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and President Xi Jinping of China.

item.title: Top White House Cybersecurity Official Is Replaced
item.description: The departure of Sean Cairncross comes after a series of technological outages affected U.S. companies and federal agencies in the past week.
item.dc:creator: Chris Cameron and Dustin Volz
item.category: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
item.media:description: Sean Cairncross in Menlo Park, Calif., earlier this week.

item.title: Technology Promised Ease. Outages Are Making Many Americans Uneasy.
item.description: The recent spate of tech disruptions has forced Americans to reckon with how dependent they have become on worldwide computer networks.
item.dc:creator: Campbell Robertson and Elizabeth Dias
item.media:description: Travelers looked at a flight information board full of canceled and delayed flights at San Francisco International Airport after a nationwide ground stop.

item.title: What You Should Know About Downdetector Before the Next Big Tech Outage
item.description: The website has been checked and cited often during an unusually busy week of technology problems, though its operators acknowledge its limitations.
item.dc:creator: Michael Levenson
item.media:credit: Sarah Rice for The New York Times
item.media:description: For many, Downdetector has become a go-to website to check for possible widespread system outages.

item.title: Anthropic Debuts on Wall Street as a $2 Trillion Company
item.description: The San Francisco company was the first major A.I. lab to go public in a highly anticipated moment for the tech industry, before ending the day valued at $1.7 trillion.
item.dc:creator: Cory Weinberg and Erin Griffith
item.media:credit: Karsten Moran for The New York Times
item.media:description: Anthropic’s co-founders and executives appeared on Nasdaq’s Times Square billboard in Manhattan as the company began trading shares on Thursday.

item.title: Anthropic’s I.P.O. Turns Tech Researchers Into Overnight Millionaires
item.description: Many people who joined the A.I. company a few years ago might have had little reason to think how big Anthropic would become. They are now worth tens of millions of dollars, if not more.
item.dc:creator: Cory Weinberg
item.media:credit: Karsten Moran for The New York Times
item.media:description: An Anthropic ad in Times Square on Thursday before the company began its first day trading.

item.title: How Much Anthropic Are You About to Own?
item.description: See how much of the stock you may own through common index funds, like those found in retirement accounts.
item.dc:creator: C.J. Robinson

item.title: Whatever You Thought Texas Was, It’s Bigger and Bluer Than That
item.description: After Democrats broke a decades-long Republican winning streak this month, Texans are reflecting on who gets to define the place they call home.
item.dc:creator: Sasha von Oldershausen and Jesus Jiménez
item.media:credit: Jordan Vonderhaar for The New York Times
item.media:description: The dome of the Texas Capitol in Austin.

item.title: Justice Department Gives Up on Alaska Senate Lawsuit
item.description: The Trump administration had sought to block certification of election results if Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, lost narrowly in his bid for re-election. Critics had called the suit meritless.
item.dc:creator: Bayliss Wagner
item.media:credit: Demetrius Freeman for The New York Times
item.media:description: Attorney General Todd Blanche in June. The Justice Department had sued Alaska at the president’s direction over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan in the race for a Senate seat in the state.

item.title: Former Biden Chief, With Help From Alex Soros, Will Gather Aides of 2028 Hopefuls
item.description: Jen O’Malley Dillon, who led the former president’s last two White House bids, is inviting top Democratic operatives to a gathering funded in part by the megadonor Alex Soros.
item.dc:creator: Reid J. Epstein and Tyler Pager
item.media:credit: Haiyun Jiang for The New York Times
item.media:description: Jen O’Malley Dillon was the campaign manager for Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s 2020 bid and became the top official on the 2024 campaign for Mr. Biden and then for Vice President Kamala Harris.

item.title: Grand Theft Auto Used to Satirize American Life. Now We’ve Caught Up With It.
item.description: The G.T.A. series is more than just a crime simulator — it’s a cartoonish sendup of our country. What happens when reality outruns the joke?
item.dc:creator: Joseph Bernstein

item.title: Amid Outcry, Army Delays its Plan to Blow Up Toxic Ammunition in Iowa
item.description: The Army had planned to detonate a cache of dangerous explosives on Friday, potentially creating a plume of toxic lead dust stretching for 60 miles. The explosion is now set for Monday.
item.dc:creator: Quinn Glabicki and Hiroko Tabuchi
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:credit: Lyndon French for The New York Times
item.media:description: The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, in 2023. A military explosive, lead azide, had been expected to be detonated there on Friday.

item.title: Senate Passes Major Permitting Bill to Speed Up Energy Projects
item.description: The bill would overhaul federal environmental laws to make it easier to build everything from gas pipelines to wind farms. But it faces hurdles in the House.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer and Olivia Diaz
item.media:credit: Nina Riggio for The New York Times
item.media:description: Power lines that carry electricity from Utah’s Intermountain Power Plant to Los Angeles run through Delta, Utah.

item.title: The Permitting Bill Is Splitting the Environmental Movement
item.description: Speeding up approvals for clean energy could help fight global warming — but many green groups fear its other provisions go too far.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer

item.title: Fiona the Hippo, Star of Cincinnati Zoo and Beyond, Dies After Eating Child’s Hat
item.description: The beloved Nile hippopotamus became ill after eating a children’s hat that accidentally ended up in her enclosure.
item.dc:creator: Remy Tumin
item.media:description: Fiona passed away after swallowing a hat that had fallen in her enclosure.

item.title: Tinto Brass Has Died. He Directed the Erotic Epic ‘Caligula.’
item.description: “The moments of lust and desire” in his movies, he said, grew “out of the stories themselves,” transcending pornography. He was 93.
item.dc:creator: Richard Sandomir
item.media:description: Tinto Brass in 1979. He was “one of the most original experimental filmmakers in Italian and international cinema during the 1960s,” one critic said.
